answer.sourceLine: These are the closing instructions of 1 Thessalonians, Paul’s letter to the church at Thessalonica — a letter usually dated to about AD 49–51 and widely regarded as the earliest surviving Christian document of any kind. The wording here is the King James Version of 1611 ↗, where it stands as verse 18 of chapter 5, verbatim.

source.excerpt: Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
trail: The verse appears verbatim in the Wikisource transcription of the King James text ↗, as chapter 5, verse 18.

It reads identically in Project Gutenberg’s King James Version of the Bible ↗, under the book heading ‘The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Thessalonians’ — an independent transcription, so the wording is not resting on one editor.
The letter itself is attributed to Paul and dated to roughly AD 49–51 ↗, written during his stay in Corinth; most scholars treat it as authentically Pauline on grounds of style and theology.
source.excerptNote: The three sentences run together in the letter as a single burst of closing instructions. Note the KJV’s ‘every thing’ as two words — both public-domain texts checked here read it that way. The one-word ‘everything’ is the spelling the quotation usually travels in.

author.name: Paul the Apostle
author.heading: About Paul the Apostle
author.metaLine: c. 5 – c. 64/65 AD · Apostle & letter-writer of the early Church
author.bio: Born Saul of Tarsus in Roman Cilicia around AD 5, Paul began as a persecutor of the first Christians and became the most prolific letter-writer of the early Church. 1 Thessalonians is generally held to be his earliest surviving letter — and therefore the oldest Christian text we have, predating the gospels. He is thought to have been executed at Rome around AD 64–65.

context.heading: Why ‘in’ is not ‘for’
lead: Paul is writing to a young, anxious congregation, and he ends the letter in staccato — rejoice, pray, give thanks — three imperatives in ten words. The instruction is to give thanks in every circumstance, not for every circumstance: thanksgiving is the posture you hold while things happen to you, not a verdict that everything happening is good.
context.detailsSummary: On ‘in every thing’ vs ‘for all things’
detailsBody: The distinction is easy to lose because a different Pauline letter does say ‘for’. Ephesians 5:20 in the same KJV text ↗ reads ‘Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ’. The two are easy to blend, and blending them is how a line about gratitude amid hardship gets repeated as a claim that hardship is itself a gift.
context.pull: Give thanks in every thing — not for every thing.

The same verse appears verbatim in Project Gutenberg's KJV, under the heading 'The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Thessalonians'; the same text gives Ephesians 5:20 as 'Giving thanks always for all things'.
1 Thessalonians is attributed to Paul, dated c. AD 49-51 during his stay in Corinth, and is widely agreed to be the earliest extant Christian text.
Paul, born Saul of Tarsus in Cilicia, lived c. 5 - c. 64/65 AD.
